props.title: Raging Bull

sections.content: Raging Bull (1980) stands as Martin Scorsese's brutal masterpiece of self-destruction, with Robert De Niro's transformative performance as Jake LaMotta defining method acting excellence. Shot in stark black and white by Michael Chapman, the film's boxing sequences revolutionized sports cinematography - the camera moves inside the ring like a third fighter, while distorted sound effects and flashbulbs create a dreamlike intensity. De Niro gained 60 pounds to play the older LaMotta, setting a new standard for physical actor commitment that influenced later transformations like Christian Bale in The Machinist (2004) and Matthew McConaughey in Dallas Buyers Club (2013).

sections.content: Scorsese and editor Thelma Schoonmaker crafted fight sequences that feel more like psychological horror than traditional sports action. The violence extends beyond the ring - LaMotta's domestic abuse and paranoid jealousy create an atmosphere of constant tension, influenced by film noir classics like The Set-Up (1949). Joe Pesci's performance as Joey LaMotta established his collaboration with Scorsese that would continue through Goodfellas (1990) and Casino (1995), perfecting the volatile supporting character type.

The film's exploration of toxic masculinity and self-loathing influenced later character studies like The Wrestler (2008) and Whiplash (2014). Its unflinching portrayal of a deeply flawed protagonist pushed boundaries for antihero narratives, paving the way for complex character studies like Taxi Driver (1976) and There Will Be Blood (2007). The final scene, with LaMotta practicing his comedy routine in a mirror, echoes the earlier boxing sequences - still fighting, but now against himself. SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation and Influence

sections.content: Scorsese's decision to shoot in black and white wasn't just aesthetic - it was partially to differentiate from Rocky (1976) and partially to preserve the film's harsh reality, as color boxing footage of the era had started to fade. The innovative sound design, mixing animal noises into fight scenes and distorting crowd noise, influenced sports films for decades. Ali (2001) and Creed (2015) both drew from Raging Bull's visceral approach to boxing choreography.
